claims.claim: 800 requests a second at p99 under 150 ms is a modest target for a read-only, indexed lookup; a few Spring Boot pods can handle it
claims.measured: Single Postgres query on 1 CPU: java-spring 7,668 rps at p99 77.87 ms; java-spring-vt 12,731 rps at p99 12.39 ms
claims.why: One 1-CPU Spring Boot container did roughly 10–16 times the 800 rps target with p99 well under 150 ms, so a few pods is plenty.

claims.claim: The database call, the connection pool and the network will decide your latency, not the language runtime
claims.about: language runtimes in general vs Spring Boot
claims.why: The benchmarks measure each server at saturation with 64 connections, not latency at a light 800 rps load, so they can't show whether the runtime's share of latency matters there.

claims.claim: Go does use less memory and starts faster
claims.measured: Start-up 238–293 ms vs 5,939 ms; idle memory 2 MB vs 134 MB; peak memory on the DB test 11–12 MB vs 499 MB (307 MB with virtual threads)
claims.why: Go measured far lower on both memory and start-up time, which matches the direction claimed.

claims.claim: That saves perhaps a few hundred MB per pod
claims.measured: Peak memory on the DB test: 12 MB vs 499 MB (about 487 MB saved), or 307 MB with virtual threads (about 295 MB saved); idle 2 MB vs 134 MB
claims.why: The measured gap under load is about 300–490 MB per container, which fits 'a few hundred MB'.

claims.measured: 293 ms vs 5,939 ms (6,224 ms with virtual threads), a difference of about 5.6–5.9 s
claims.why: The measured start-up difference is several seconds.

claims.claim: Go's benefits are real but small at this load
claims.measured: Single query: go-gin 22,138 rps at p99 6.00 ms vs java-spring 7,668 rps at p99 77.87 ms and java-spring-vt 12,731 rps at p99 12.39 ms
claims.why: Go is faster, but both stacks exceed 800 rps by a wide margin, so the advantage is real but doesn't matter at this load.

claims.claim: Spring Boot with GraalVM native image gets you Go-like footprint and startup
Quarkus or Micronaut are lighter than Spring Boot
claims.why: Neither Quarkus nor Micronaut was benchmarked.

claims.claim: Spring WebFlux (reactive) is not needed at 800 rps
claims.why: WebFlux wasn't measured, though the servlet stack's results suggest it handles 800 rps easily.

claims.claim: Virtual threads suit blocking JDBC calls under bursty load
claims.measured: Single query: 12,731 vs 7,668 rps, p99 12.39 vs 77.87 ms; 20 queries: 1,699 vs 1,254 rps, p99 94.16 vs 236.30 ms
claims.why: On the DB tests, virtual threads gave higher throughput and much lower p99 than platform threads.

claims.claim: JVM pods that have just started have slow first requests (cold start and warm-up)
claims.measured: Start-up 5,939 ms; warm-up behaviour not measured (excluded by the 5 s warm-up period)
claims.why: The benchmark leaves out the first 5 s of traffic, so it says nothing about how slow the first requests are.

claims.claim: Under-provisioned CPU on OpenShift is a common cause of JVM p99 spikes
claims.why: The measurements don't vary CPU limits and don't cover OpenShift.

claims.claim: At this load, I don't expect a benchmark will find Spring Boot misses the target
claims.measured: Single query on 1 CPU: 7,668 rps at p99 77.87 ms (java-spring-vt 12,731 rps at p99 12.39 ms)
claims.why: Even at saturation on one CPU, Spring Boot beat both the 800 rps and the 150 ms p99 targets.
